intro: Five of these forty-one stand in the Prinsentuin, which has been an open public walking park for more than two hundred years and is one of the first in the Netherlands. It was laid out between 1822 and 1824 on the old northern ramparts by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the Frisian garden architect who also designed the city cemetery a few streets north, where herons now nest in the crowns of his plane trees. The oldest, and the one to see first, is a copper beech by the Westerkerk that the register says will eventually have to come down.
meta_description: Forty-one trees in Leeuwarden: five in the two-hundred-year-old Prinsentuin, a heron colony in a Roodbaard cemetery, and a beech on borrowed time.
question_meta: Leeuwarden's oldest tree is a copper beech by the Westerkerk, banded 1750 to 1800, and the register expects it will have to be felled.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Leeuwarden is a copper beech standing by the Westerkerk on the Sint Anthonystraat, which the national register places in a planting band of 1750 to 1800, so between about 225 and 275 years old. It is also the one tree here with a warning attached. The register records that its rooting ground was compacted in the 1990s, that the tree took a blow from which it never recovered, and that although the ground has since been improved its condition has not come back, so it will in time have to be felled. It is standing now. If you want to see the oldest tree in Leeuwarden, this is an argument for going this year rather than in ten.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every age on this page is a band and none is narrowed to look precise. The register is the 2024 edition and is the single source for most of these trees, which is why they are flagged. It is a careful source: for several of these it records the tree's condition as well as its age, which is where the note about the Westerkerk beech comes from and why we have passed it on rather than quietly leaving it out. The Prinsentuin trees are dated indirectly, because the register reasons from the park's own history that the oldest trees in it must come from between 1830 and 1880 rather than from a record of any individual planting. Pins are as the register surveyed them; where one is marked approximate we know the park and not the trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Leeuwarden?
faq.a: A copper beech by the Westerkerk, banded 1750 to 1800. The register notes that its growing ground was compacted in the 1990s and its condition never recovered, and that it will eventually have to be felled.

It has been a public walking park for over two hundred years, which makes it one of the earliest in the Netherlands. The present layout was made between 1822 and 1824 in the existing garden on the former northern fortifications, by the Frisian garden architect Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, in the romantic style. The rampart and canal system it belongs to has been a national monument since 1967.

faq.q: Is there really a heron colony in the old cemetery?
faq.a: Yes. The Oude Stadsbegraafplaats on the Jelsummerstraat was laid out in 1833 to a Roodbaard design, is no longer in use and is a national monument. Grey herons nest in the crowns of its old trees and many of the trunks are grown over with ivy.

Yes. The Prinsentuin is an open public park, the old cemetery is open ground and no longer in use, and the Westerkerk beech stands on the street. The horse chestnut at Poptaslot, out at Marssum, stands in a garden that is free but keeps weekday hours, April to September, and is closed on Sundays. The Cedar of Lebanon at the Gabbema Gasthuis is one to see from the street: the gate there is open to people on foot, but nobody has confirmed whether the almshouse grounds themselves are public.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Prinsentuin
trees.age_estimate: roughly 195 to 205 years, from the register's planting band of 1820 to 1830

location.address: Prinsentuin, Groeneweg 1, beside the Historisch Centrum

trees.story:
This tree is almost exactly as old as the idea of a public park in this country.

Between 1822 and 1824 the city had a new garden laid out on the northern fortifications, in the existing grounds, by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the Frisian garden architect who spent his career converting Dutch formality into the romantic English manner: curved paths, water, planned views, no straight lines. It has been open to the public ever since, which makes the Prinsentuin one of the first public walking parks in the Netherlands and this chestnut one of the original plantings.

Two hundred years of people walking under a tree is not neutral. Horse chestnuts suffer badly from compacted ground and this one has had two centuries of feet. It is also the species now under attack across Europe from the leaf miner moth, which browns the foliage from July onward and makes a mature chestnut look half dead by August without actually killing it.

So come in May, when it is at its unarguable best: white candles held upright all over the crown, in a park laid out by a man who would have chosen it for exactly that.

It stands beside the Historisch Centrum, on the Groeneweg side.
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The big chestnut on the Groeneweg side of the park, next to the Historisch Centrum. In May it is covered in upright white flower spikes.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles are up across the whole crown

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Westerkerk
trees.age_estimate: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800

location.address: By the Westerkerk, Sint Anthonystraat 3

trees.story:
The national register does not usually tell you a tree is going to die. About this one it does.

In the 1990s the ground it roots in was compacted, which for a beech is close to the worst thing that can be done to it: the fine feeding roots sit in the top half metre of soil and they need air in it. The tree took a blow it never came back from. The ground has since been improved and its condition has not recovered, and the register states plainly that it will in time have to be felled.

It is the oldest tree in Leeuwarden, banded 1750 to 1800, standing by a church whose history runs back to the fifteenth century and which has been reworked repeatedly for the different uses it has been put to.

There is nothing tragic to look at. A declining old beech is still an enormous dark thing on a city street, and the decline is mostly visible in what is missing: thinner cover at the top of the crown, more light coming through than there should be, dead ends on the upper branches.

This is the only tree on this site we would tell you to see sooner rather than later.
trees.access: Free. Stands on the street by the church, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 800 m north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The large purple-leaved beech beside the Westerkerk on the Sint Anthonystraat, with a noticeably thin upper crown.

trees.name: The Beech at the Pier Pander Temple
trees.age_estimate: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850

location.address: Prinsentuin, at the Pier Pander temple

trees.story:
There is a small classical temple in this park, built in 1924 to hold the work of one sculptor.

Pier Pander was born in Friesland in 1864, the son of a rag merchant, and got out through talent and patronage: Rome, a career in marble, and an early death in 1919. The temple was raised to his own plans five years later, a domed round building in a public park, to house his sculpture. There are not many Dutch artists with a temple.

The beech stands beside it. Its date is not certain: the register bands it 1840 to 1850 and notes that trees here could equally have gone in when the temple was built, but photographs from the 1930s argue for the earlier reading. This is the Noorderplantage, laid out in 1843 on the former Noorderdwinger bastion and joined to the Prinsentuin at its eastern end, and the register's general conclusion is that the oldest trees in it date from between 1830 and 1880.

A beech beside a domed white building is a deliberate effect: smooth grey bark against smooth stone, and in summer a canopy dense enough to put the whole temple in shade.
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The beech standing against the small domed temple at the western end of the park.

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.name: The Plane of the Old City Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850

location.address: Oude Stadsbegraafplaats, Jelsummerstraat, on the path between sections 2 and 3

trees.story:
Grey herons nest in the tops of these trees.

That is the first thing to know about the old city cemetery, and in February and March it is loud. Herons are colonial breeders, they choose tall trees near water, they start early in the year, and a heronry is not a quiet place: a large ragged nest per fork, birds arriving with sticks, and a noise like an argument in a shed. From below you mostly see the undersides and hear the rest.

The ground was laid out in 1833 to a design by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the same architect as the Prinsentuin, which is why a cemetery here reads like a landscape garden with graves in it. It went out of use long ago and is now a national monument. Ivy has taken many of the trunks.

The plane is on the path between sections two and three, banded 1840 to 1850, so from the earliest planting. London plane is the classic city tree because it sheds its bark in plates and with it the soot, which is why the trunk is a camouflage of cream, olive and grey.

Go in early spring, before the leaves, when you can see the birds.
trees.access: Free. Open ground, no longer in use as a cemetery.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Leeuwarden station, on the Jelsummerstraat.
trees.how_to_recognise: Flaking cream and olive bark, on the path between sections 2 and 3. In late winter, the tree with heron nests in the top.

best_time.label: March, bare, with the heron colony visible in the crowns

trees.name: The Beech behind Tresoar
trees.age_estimate: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870

location.address: Prinsentuin, behind the library building

trees.story:
It stands next to the building where Friesland keeps its memory.

Tresoar is the Frisian historical and literary centre, the archive of a language with its own literature and its own long argument about being a language. The beech is directly behind it, in the Prinsentuin, on the line of the old northern fortifications that the park was built on and that have been a national monument since 1967.

The register bands it 1860 to 1870, which places it a generation after Roodbaard's layout rather than in it, planted into a park that already existed.

Beech is the tree that makes a Dutch park feel like a wood. It casts the heaviest shade of any large tree here, dense enough that almost nothing grows under a mature one, so the ground beneath is bare orange leaf litter and roots. That is not neglect, it is the tree winning.

Run your hand over the trunk. Beech bark stays smooth and thin its whole life, which is why people carve it, and why an old one in a public park usually carries a century of initials that have stretched and blurred as the trunk widened.
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: Smooth grey trunk, bare ground beneath, directly behind the library building.

best_time.label: October, when it turns copper and the litter goes orange

trees.name: The Ash by the Tea House
trees.age_estimate: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880

location.address: Prinsentuin, on the bank by the Theekoepel

trees.story:
The register calls this a very impressive specimen of the species and then adds, in the same breath, that its crown has developed one-sidedly because of the park trees standing next to it.

Both are true and the second explains the first. A tree that grows up hemmed in on one side puts everything it has into the open side, so you end up with an asymmetric crown reaching out over the path or the water, which reads as dramatic rather than damaged. Roodbaard's successors planted a park; the trees then negotiated among themselves.

It stands on the bank by the Theekoepel, the tea house, in the Noorderplantage end of the grounds, and the register bands it 1870 to 1880.

An ash of that age is worth stopping for now more than it was twenty years ago. Ash dieback, a fungal disease that arrived in the Netherlands in 2010, has killed a large share of the country's ash in the years since, and a tolerant mature tree is no longer an ordinary thing. A minority resist it, apparently on genetics rather than luck, and every big healthy one left is a candidate.

Black buds in winter, in opposite pairs. Nothing else here has them.
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: A big ash with a lopsided crown leaning away from its neighbours, on the slope by the tea house. Matt black buds in winter.

trees.name: The Marilandica Poplar
trees.age_estimate: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880

location.address: Prinsentuin, centrally, by the Noorder Stadsgracht

trees.story:
The trunk is the reason to come. It is deeply grooved and covered in burrs, hard woody swellings the size of fists and heads, which on a poplar of this age turn the bole into something closer to rock than bark.

Burrs are the tree's response to damage or infection: a knot of dormant buds that keeps growing without ever making a shoot, laying down wildly disordered grain. Woodturners prize the timber for exactly that and pay serious money for a burr this size. Standing on a public park bank by a city canal is the safest place it could be.

Marilandica is a named clone of the Canadian poplar, the hybrid of European black poplar and American cottonwood, selected and propagated by cuttings, which means every Marilandica anywhere is genetically the same tree. This one has been growing since the 1870s at the centre of the Prinsentuin by the Noorder Stadsgracht.

Poplars are planted for speed and taken out early because they get brittle. This one has been left, and a century and a half of being left is what produced the trunk.

Go and put your hands on it. That is the whole visit.
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: Centrally in the park by the canal, the tree with a deeply furrowed trunk covered in large woody burrs.

trees.name: The Feather Elms of Molenstraat
trees.age_estimate: about 90 to 95 years (planted 1930 to 1940)

location.address: Molenstraat, opposite house numbers 29 and 35, Leeuwarden

trees.story:
The graft on this street elm has swollen into a collar of scar tissue with a circumference of more than five metres, wider at that single point than the trunk of almost anything else on this list.

Two feather elms, a narrow, upright cultivar of wych elm, stand about ten metres apart in an ordinary two by two metre planting pit on a residential street. Both were grafted roughly 1.5 metres above the ground when they were planted, a standard way to propagate this cultivar, and in the ninety-odd years since, the graft union on the larger of the two has ballooned far beyond the trunk it sits on.

An oak fern has taken root in the crown of that same tree, an epiphyte quietly living in the canopy of a street planting that most passersby probably read as unremarkable. The Dutch national register of monumental trees lists the pair under its dendrological category: official recognition for two elms that most of Molenstraat likely walks past without a second look.
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (LRMB), entry nr 1682944, 'Pluimiepen Molenstraat'
trees.access: Free. Public street, always accessible.
trees.transport: About 1.2 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: Two tall, narrow elms opposite house numbers 29 and 35. The larger of the pair carries a huge swollen collar about 1.5 metres up the trunk, where it was grafted.

trees.name: The White Horse Chestnut of Poptaslot
trees.age_estimate: roughly 185 years

location.address: Slotleane, Poptaslot (Heringastate), Marssum
location.neighbourhood: Front/side garden of Poptaslot, a 17th-century almshouse estate near Leeuwarden, about 4km from Leeuwarden's published lee_003

trees.story:
Left to itself, this horse chestnut would surround itself with children. Its lowest branches sweep down to the grass and will root wherever they rest, throwing up a ring of new stems around the parent trunk. The gardener at Poptaslot cuts them back so the tree stays one tree.

It was planted in 1840 by L.P. Roodbaard, the landscape architect who redrew country estate after country estate across Friesland in the loose English style, as part of his design for the grounds here. Three maples nearby are his too, the same year, the same job. Poptaslot, also called Heringastate, was already a seventeenth century almshouse estate when he arrived, so the chestnut has spent its whole life as the newest thing on old ground.

The trunk is 4.75 metres round and the tree is 19 metres tall. In June 2017 the national tree foundation put it first on its list of the ten most beautiful trees in Friesland, ahead of older and larger trees. Not the oldest, not the biggest, just the one people wanted to stand under.

The garden is free, on weekdays from April to September, roughly nine to four and later in high summer, closed on Sundays. Going inside the house is a guided tour and a separate arrangement, but the tree is in the garden and the garden is the free part.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles come out all over the crown

trees.access: Free. The garden, where the tree stands, is open on weekdays from April to September (roughly 09:00-16:00, later in July and August) and closed on Sundays. Seeing inside the house itself is a separate, paid tour.
trees.transport: Village of Marssum, near Leeuwarden; reachable by local bus, roughly 10-15 minutes from Leeuwarden centre by car.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its lowest branches swept down to the grass, cut back to stop them rooting into a ring of new stems. It stands in the garden of Poptaslot, near Marssum.

trees.name: The Wilhelminaboom
trees.age_estimate: about 128 years, planted in 1898

location.address: Raadhuisplein, in front of the old town hall, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1684252, 'Hollandse linde Wilhelminaboom', planted band 1890-1900)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, stop 4)
trees.access: Free, on the public Raadhuisplein square in front of the old town hall (het Stadhuis); the tree stands inside an ornamental iron fence but the square itself is open at all times.
trees.transport: About 600m (roughly 8 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station; in the city centre.
trees.story:
Most commemorative trees get a plaque. This one got a fence carrying the state sword, the sceptre and the orb.

The lime went into the Raadhuisplein in 1898, the year Wilhelmina took the throne at eighteen, and the city set the architect Hendrik Kramer to work on the ironwork around its bed. Gates face each street that meets the square. Crowned letter W's and halberds stand along the rails, with orange twigs, blossom and apples worked into the metal between them. It is a great deal of blacksmithing for one lime, and it tells you precisely how a small provincial capital felt about its new queen.

A tinted postcard from around 1910 shows the result a decade in: a young tree inside a fence that already looks the more permanent of the two. The fence has not changed since. The tree has had a century and a quarter to catch up.

The date holds up from two directions. The city's own monumental-green walking route puts the planting at 1898, and the national register separately lists a Hollandse linde at this coordinate with a planting band of 1890 to 1900.

Fifty years later Leeuwarden planted a second royal lime a few hundred metres north, for Wilhelmina's daughter Juliana. Both are still standing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the ornamental iron fence around its bed, worked with crowned W's, halberds and the state sword, sceptre and orb. It stands alone on the Raadhuisplein, in front of the old town hall.

best_time.label: late June and early July, when the lime flowers and the scent hangs over the square

trees.name: The Julianaboom
trees.age_estimate: about 78 years, planted in 1948

location.address: Jacobijnerkerkhof, near the entrance to the Boshuizen Gasthuis, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1683830, 'Hollandse linde Julianaboom', planted band 1940-1950)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, stop 7 and top-10 entry IX)
trees.access: Free, in the public square around the Jacobijnerkerk (Grote Kerk); the tree stands in a rectangular bed in the north-west corner of the churchyard, open at all times.
trees.transport: About 850m (roughly 11 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station; in the city centre.
trees.story:
Leeuwarden's official list of its ten most special trees includes one that people now living watched go into the ground.

A photograph from 1948 shows alderman M.H. Geerts with a spade in front of the double gateway of the Boshuisen Gasthuis. The lime he is planting is still there, in the same rectangular bed in the north-west corner of the Jacobijnerkerkhof, and it carries the name of Princess Juliana. The country was three years out of the German occupation. The city planted a tree for the heir to the throne and had the alderman photographed doing it.

At 78 it is young for a register that mostly deals in centuries, and the national register does carry it: a Hollandse linde at this coordinate, planting band 1940 to 1950, which is about as close to a countersignature on the 1948 date as a register gets.

Behind it stands the gateway of the Boshuisen Gasthuis, an almshouse founded in 1652 by Anna van Eysinga, which makes the lime by nearly three centuries the newest thing on the corner. The Jacobijnerkerk takes up the rest of the square.

Two limes, two queens, fifty years and a few hundred metres apart, and both still standing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the rectangular bed it stands in on its own, in the north-west corner of the churchyard around the Jacobijnerkerk. It stands in front of the double gateway of the Boshuisen Gasthuis.

best_time.label: late June and early July, when it flowers and the churchyard fills with the sound of bees

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Noorderweg
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 to 127 years

location.address: Noorderweg, beside the walking path near the Noorderbrug and the Stedelijk Gymnasium, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1682934, 'Witte paardenkastanje Noorderbrug', planted band 1900-1910)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, top-10 entry III, dated 1899)
trees.access: Free, beside the public walking path along the Noorderweg/Arendstuin between the Noorderbrug and the Stedelijk Gymnasium.
trees.transport: About 1.1km (roughly 13 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station.
trees.story:
This chestnut made the city's top ten on the strength of one branch.

The monumental-green walking route that the gemeente publishes with the Historisch Centrum names ten trees as Leeuwarden's most special, and the entry for this one turns almost entirely on a single zware gesteltak: a heavy, low main limb that leaves the trunk and reaches out over the footpath. You meet it on the far side of the Stedelijk Gymnasium, on the stretch of the Noorderweg between the Noorderbrug and the flower shop Blomke fan Romke.

The two sources do not quite agree on when it went in. The brochure says 1899. The national register, which carries it as a witte paardenkastanje by the Noorderbrug, gives a planting band of 1900 to 1910. The disagreement is a year or so wide and settles nothing important: this is a tree from the turn of the twentieth century, so somewhere between 116 and 127 years old.

It has been putting that limb out over the path for longer than anyone now walking under it has been alive, through two wars, the arrival of the cars and every set of schoolchildren the gymnasium has sent past.

In May the crown goes up in white candles, the low limb included, which is the week to look at the branch that got it listed.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the one heavy limb that leaves the trunk low down and reaches out over the footpath, well below the rest of the crown. It stands on the Noorderweg between the Noorderbrug and the Stedelijk Gymnasium.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles stand up across the whole crown, low limb included

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Stationsplein
trees.age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years

location.address: Stationsplein, Leeuwarden (in front of the railway station)

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1682915, 'Oosterse plataan Stationsplein', planted band 1900-1910)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, top-10 entry V, dated circa 1900)
trees.access: Free, on the public square directly in front of Leeuwarden railway station.
trees.transport: At Leeuwarden Centraal station, on the station square itself.
trees.story:
Step off the train at Leeuwarden and the first old tree you meet is the wrong plane.

Almost every plane on a Dutch square is a London plane, the hybrid bred for city air and planted by the thousand. This one is the parent species, an Oriental plane, which is rare this far north and which the national register carries under its Dutch name, oosterse plataan, at the Stationsplein.

It has held the open ground in front of the station since about 1900. Both sources that carry it agree: the city's own list of its ten most special trees dates it circa 1900, and the register gives a planting band of 1900 to 1910, so it is somewhere between 116 and 126 years old. The crown has spread the way planes on open squares do, low and wide over the paving, with the station front behind it.

Which means every arrival in this city by rail for more than a century has walked past it, most of them watching the clock rather than the tree. It stood there through the war and through the century of traffic that has crossed this square since.

Nobody has taped its girth. If you have a tape measure and a few minutes between trains, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad, low-spreading crown standing on its own out in the open paving. It stands on the Stationsplein directly in front of the railway station, with the station building behind it.

trees.name: The Variegated Maple of Rengerspark
trees.age_estimate: about 122 years, planted around 1904

location.address: Rengerspark, just inside the entrance on Spanjaardslaan, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1695808, 'Bontbladige esdoorn Rengerspark', planted band 1900-1910)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, top-10 entry VI, dated 1904)
trees.access: Free, inside the public Rengerspark (a former private gift to the city, opened 1904, rijksmonument since 2001), just left of the entrance gate on Spanjaardslaan.
trees.transport: About 1.2km (roughly 15 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station.
trees.story:
The park gate carries 1904 in its ironwork, and so, near enough, does the tree standing just inside it.

Rengerspark was a private gift. In 1902 the former mayor W.J. van Welderen baron Rengers and his wife handed the ground to the city, Hendrik Copijn laid it out, and it opened in 1904 with more than fifty labelled tree species in it. A few steps inside the entrance on the Spanjaardslaan stands a sycamore of the cultivar 'Leopoldii', which the city's list of its ten most special trees names outright and dates to that opening year. The national register agrees within a decade: a bontbladige esdoorn on the south side of the park, planting band 1900 to 1910.

Spring is when the cultivar earns its place. The new leaves come out mottled pink, cream and green rather than plain green, as though somebody had been careless with the paint, and they hold that colouring for weeks before darkening. Nothing about it is accidental. Somebody choosing the trees for a brand new park in 1904 wanted a maple that would do this at the gate, and 122 years later it still does.

The park became a rijksmonument in 2001, which put Copijn's layout under protection. The maple has stood through the whole of it, and through the two wars that came in between.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, mottled pink, cream and green rather than plain green. It stands just inside the park's Spanjaardslaan entrance gate, the one whose ironwork carries the year 1904.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open mottled pink and cream before they darken

location.address: Willemskade 27, along the garden boundary facing the street, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1682937, 'Bruine beuk stadsvilla Willemskade', planted band 1860-1870, designated by the municipality and entered in the national register in 1988)

https://www.ivn.nl/afdeling/leeuwarden-eo/leren-over-de-natuur/wandelen-langs-monumentale-bomen-in-leeuwarden/ (IVN Leeuwarden e.o., 'Wandelen langs monumentale bomen in Leeuwarden', names two brown beeches at Willemskade 27, dated circa 1865)
trees.access: Free to view from Willemskade street; the tree stands in the garden of a private 19th-century villa (a national heritage building, built 1874) along the boundary facing the street. Register marks it visitable=ja and visible=ja.
trees.transport: About 1km south of Leeuwarden Centraal station, along the Willemskade waterfront.
trees.story:
For most of its life this beech was half of something else.

Two copper beeches went into the garden at Willemskade 27 around 1865, close enough together that over the decades they grew into and through one another. The IVN's walking guide to Leeuwarden's monumental trees calls them relatiebomen and still describes a pair. That guide has been overtaken. The national register's own history for the entry records that the southern tree was felled in 2026 after a fungus weakened its base, a problem first written up at an inspection in 2023. The northern beech is the one left standing, and it is the one on this page.

It was in the ground before the house was. The villa behind it, now a listed building, went up in 1874; the register gives the trees a planting band of 1860 to 1870 and the IVN says circa 1865, which puts this one at roughly 160 years old. The municipality designated it and entered it in the national register in 1988.

You look at it from the pavement. It stands along the garden boundary facing the Willemskade, on private ground with a public view, which is how the waterfront has seen it for a century and a half. In late April the new leaves open translucent red before they darken, and for a fortnight the whole crown holds the light.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its dark purple leaves, the single beech now left on the garden boundary at Willemskade 27, where a fused pair stood until 2026. It faces the street, in front of the 1874 villa.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Vosseparkje
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years

location.address: Westerpark / Vosseparkje, west side, Leeuwarden

trees.access: Free, public park (Westerpark/Vosseparkje), open daily
trees.transport: Short walk from Leeuwarden centre; the park sits just west of the Prinsentuin cluster
trees.story:
An ice storm in March 1987 damaged this wingnut badly enough that the scar is still visible behind an old branch, and decades on it is one of two enormous trees flanking the path where Vosseparkje opens onto Molenstraat.

The Caucasian wingnut is native to forests around the Caspian Sea, thousands of kilometres from Friesland. Leeuwarden's own specimen has grown a trunk 130 centimetres round, a figure the national tree register does not even record: it comes from a walking-tour pamphlet published by the city's own historical centre, which found the tree standing beside a second, gold-leaved companion nobody has identified yet.

The park itself dates to 1872, laid out by garden architect Gerrit Vlaskamp around a drinking-water reservoir the city needed more than it needed a park, and the wingnut went in a generation later, sometime between 1900 and 1910. It has outlived the reservoir's original purpose, the ice storm, and watched the technical school built beside the park in 1936 grow old itself.

Two sources place it slightly differently, one at the Molenstraat path junction and one on the park's west side, close enough that this reads as one tree rather than two, but worth a second look on the ground.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 130 centimetres round, and by the gold-leaved companion tree growing right beside it. It stands where the park path meets Molenstraat, near the old MTS school building.

trees.name: The Grey Poplar of Vosseparkje
trees.age_estimate: 117 years (planted 1909)

location.address: Westerpark / Vosseparkje, east side of the pond, Leeuwarden

trees.access: Free, public park (Westerpark/Vosseparkje), open daily
trees.transport: Short walk from Leeuwarden centre; the park sits just west of the Prinsentuin cluster
trees.story:
A Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden walking brochure and the national tree register agree down to the year: this grey poplar on the east side of Vosseparkje's pond went into the ground in 1909, one of the exotic and unusual trees the brochure singles out on a route otherwise lined with white and red horse chestnuts.

It survived the storm of 1970 that flattened trees across the Netherlands and remains, in the register's own words, healthy and structurally sound more than a century later. The species is a hybrid of white poplar and aspen, common enough as roadside planting but rarely old enough to earn a place in a national monumental-trees register.

It stands on the pond's east bank in Westerpark, known locally as Vosseparkje, alongside a leaning white acacia the same brochure records as propped up nearby, and, on the park's far side, a Caucasian wingnut with a trunk more than a metre round. Together they form the park's own cluster of registered trees, a short walk from the Prinsentuin and Princessehof gardens where most of Leeuwarden's other old trees stand.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, on the east bank of Vosseparkje's pond, among white and red horse chestnuts, paper birches and a blue Atlas cedar the brochure lists nearby.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of the Beursgebouw
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years

location.address: Wirdumerdijk 34, in front of the former Beursgebouw, opposite the Campus Fryslan (Rijksuniversiteit Groningen) building, Leeuwarden

trees.access: Free, public square (Wirdumerdijk, in front of the former Beursgebouw), open at all times
trees.transport: Central Leeuwarden, short walk from the Waagplein/Nieuwestad shopping area
trees.story:
The plane tree in front of Leeuwarden's former stock exchange spent years hemmed in by brick paving before the city dug it back out in 2005 and built a proper rooting structure around the trunk. Inspectors called its condition merely adequate for years afterward; by 2022 they wrote that it was clearly thriving.

The Beursgebouw behind it went up in 1880 for the city's grain and commodity traders and now houses part of the University of Groningen's Campus Fryslan. The tree came a generation later, planted sometime between 1900 and 1910 on what was then a green strip beside the building. A local nature guide's walking route singles it out for the fountain beside it and for the spiky seed balls the species drops each year.

It is not Leeuwarden's only oriental plane. A second one, planted around the same years, stands 800 metres away in front of the railway station. This one is the one with the fountain and the old trading floor at its back, on Wirdumerdijk, in the middle of the old town rather than at its edge.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fountain beside it, in front of the former Beursgebouw on Wirdumerdijk. Leeuwarden's other oriental plane stands 800 metres away at the railway station, not here.

trees.name: The Red Horse Chestnuts of the Diakonessenhuis Garden
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Diaconessenpark, off Noordersingel (former Diakonessenziekenhuis garden)

trees.story:
The hospital this chestnut was planted for closed in 1987. The tree stayed.

Leeuwarden's Diakonessenhuis was founded in 1879 and the red horse chestnut in its garden went in during the decade that followed, somewhere between 1880 and 1890, which puts it at roughly 135 to 145 years old. It was entered in the national monumental-trees register in 1989, two years after the hospital shut and while the wards around it were being turned into flats.

That conversion nearly cost it. The register's own history records the damage done by the building work of the 1990s, in particular a garage entrance dug in beside the neighbouring block, straight through ground the roots had held for a century. The tree carries two crown anchors and a wound in its trunk. Inspectors in 2017 rated its condition reasonable, which for a tree that has been through all that is a decent verdict.

The garden it stands in was laid out in 1895 to a Vlaskamp design, and the city's own monumental-green walking route notes that a few of its trees are still here. This is one of them. The register lists three trees under this entry while its own history text describes a single chestnut, so expect one tree, possibly with company.

In May the flowers come up pink rather than white, which is the entire point of the hybrid.
trees.access: Free. Stands in a landscaped courtyard now called Diaconessenpark, inside the 1990s apartment redevelopment of the former Diakonessenhuis hospital grounds. OSM maps this whole courtyard as leisure=park with paved, wheelchair-accessible footways running past the trees and a public bench right beside them, and shows no gate or private-access tag anywhere in the courtyard, only two low (0.6m) garden walls. The LRMB register itself lists this tree as owner=particulier (likely the apartment building's owners' association rather than the municipality) but visitable=ja and visible=ja. Reads as a residential courtyard rather than a destination park, but the paths through it are open.
trees.transport: About 900 m north of Leeuwarden station, on foot, just off Noordersingel.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the pink flowers in May, where the chestnuts about 30 metres east of it flower white, and by the steel cables anchoring its crown. It stands in the Diaconessenpark courtyard off Noordersingel.

best_time.label: May, when the candles come up pink instead of white

trees.name: The White Horse Chestnuts of the Diakonessenhuis Garden
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Diaconessenpark, off Noordersingel (former Diakonessenziekenhuis garden)

trees.story:
The register does not soften it: the thicker of these two chestnuts has a cavity with a fungal infection and a strong case of bleeding canker, and the condition of both is rated moderate.

They are still standing, and they have been standing a while. Both went into the garden of the Diakonessenhuis when the hospital was founded in 1879, or within the decade after it, which puts them at roughly 135 to 145 years. They were entered in the national monumental-trees register in 1989. Between those two dates the hospital closed, its wards became apartments, and the building work of the 1990s dug a garage entrance in beside them.

Bleeding canker is the bacterial disease that has been working through Europe's horse chestnuts since the early 2000s, leaving dark sticky streaks down the bark. Trees carry it for years, and some of them come back from it. Neither the register nor anyone else has written these two off.

So this is a pair to see now rather than eventually, which is an unusual thing to be able to say about a tree that predates every building around it. They stand about 30 metres east of the courtyard's pink-flowering red chestnut, in a garden laid out in 1895 to a Vlaskamp design and kept, in part, through everything that has happened to this site since.
trees.access: Free. Same courtyard as lee_019 (Diaconessenpark), about 30 m away. OSM shows the same open, paved, gate-free footway network through this stretch of the courtyard.
trees.transport: About 900 m north of Leeuwarden station, on foot, just off Noordersingel.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by standing as a pair, both flowering white in May, the thicker of the two carrying an open cavity in its trunk. They stand in the Diaconessenpark courtyard, east of the pink-flowering chestnut.

trees.name: The London Plane of the Diakonessenhuis Garden
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Diaconessenpark, off Noordersingel (former Diakonessenziekenhuis garden)

trees.story:
London planes were the tree Victorian cities planted when they wanted something that could stand the air, and they manage it by shedding their bark in plates, taking the grime off with it.

This one is the northernmost of the three registered trees in the old Diakonessenhuis garden and the closest to the hospital building itself, which means it has had the best view of everything that happened here. The hospital opened in 1879. The plane went into the ground between 1880 and 1890, so it is roughly 135 to 145 years old. The hospital closed in 1987, the building came through the years as a national monument and now holds flats, and the plane was entered in the monumental-trees register in 1989, in the middle of the conversion.

Like the chestnuts beside it, it took damage from the building work of the 1990s, when a garage entrance went in next to the neighbouring block. Inspectors rated its condition reasonable in 2017.

The register is divided about this courtyard in an odd way. The two chestnuts are listed as privately owned and openly visitable, while the plane is down to a public body with its visitability marked unknown. On the ground it is one landscaped garden with paved paths running through it and a bench beside the trees, laid out in 1895 to a Vlaskamp design and half surviving.
trees.access: Free. Same courtyard (Diaconessenpark), the northernmost of the three trees, closest to the historic hospital building itself (now apartments). Same open, paved-footway, no-gate picture from OSM as the other two.
trees.transport: About 900 m north of Leeuwarden station, on foot, just off Noordersingel.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flaking, patchwork bark, which nothing else here has, and by where it stands: the northernmost of the courtyard's three big trees, the one closest to the old hospital building.

trees.name: The Crimean Linden of Blokhuisplein
trees.age_estimate: roughly 70 to 75 years, from a documented planting date of 1954

location.address: Blokhuisplein, beside the entrance to Blokhuispoort

trees.story:
You walk past this lime to get into the public library, and you do it through the gate of the old prison.

The Blokhuispoort is Leeuwarden's jail, brick wings and barred windows, out of that use and now holding the library, a cultural venue and shops. The Crimean lime stands to the left of the entrance. The city's own monumental-green walking route dates it to 1954 and counts it among the ten trees it considers Leeuwarden's most remarkable, which it manages while being younger than most of the trees it shares that list with.

Tilia x euchlora is not the lime you usually meet on a Dutch street. It is a hybrid with darker, glossier leaves than the common lime, and part of the reason planners choose it is that it spares the pavement below the sticky honeydew rain that falls from a common lime in summer. In front of a public building on a square full of terrace seating, that is not an accident.

One caution about the pin. The only source carrying this tree is the brochure, which places it left of the Blokhuispoort entrance, and our coordinate is the geocoded centre of Blokhuisplein rather than the trunk. Walk to the entrance and look left. If you find it, tell us exactly where it stands.
trees.access: Free. Stands on or immediately beside Blokhuisplein, the public square in front of Blokhuispoort, the former prison now used as a public library, cultural venue and shops.
trees.transport: About 700 m south of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small, glossy, dark green leaves, shinier than the common limes elsewhere in the city. It stands on Blokhuisplein, to the left of the entrance to the Blokhuispoort.
trees.why_go: A lime of a species rarely planted in this country, standing at the door of Leeuwarden's old prison, which is now the city library, a cultural venue and shops. The city puts it on its own list of the ten trees most worth walking to here.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at the Gabbema Gasthuis
trees.age_estimate: roughly 118 to 122 years, from a documented planting date of 1906

location.address: In front of the Gabbema Gasthuis, Wijbrand de Geeststraat 42

trees.story:
A cedar from the mountains of Lebanon has stood in front of a Frisian almshouse since the year the almshouse was finished.

The Gabbema Gasthuis on the Wijbrand de Geeststraat was completed in 1906 to a design by Willem Cornelis de Groot, in the mixed Art Nouveau and neo-Renaissance manner of that moment, and the city's monumental-green walking route dates the cedar to the same year. It counts the tree among the ten it considers Leeuwarden's most remarkable.

Two honest notes before you go. Our coordinate is a geocode of the almshouse building rather than of the trunk, so it is good to about forty metres. And the tree stands in front of the gasthuis rather than inside it. The gate at that point is marked as one pedestrians may use, but nobody has stated in so many words that the grounds are open, so plan on seeing it from the street and treat anything more as a bonus.

From the pavement it is unmistakable anyway. Cedrus libani holds its branches out in flat, layered tiers, a shape no Dutch street tree has, and it keeps its dark needles through the winter when everything around it is bare. At about 120 years it is barely started. The trees this species is famous for, on the Lebanese mountainsides, are counted in centuries rather than decades.
trees.access: Free to view; likely on the public street frontage rather than inside the almshouse's own grounds. The brochure says the tree stands 'voor het Gabbema Gasthuis' (in front of the almshouse), which reads as street-facing rather than an interior courtyard, and OSM tags a gate right at this spot as access=permissive, foot=yes, i.e. pedestrians are allowed through it. Flagged rather than fully confirmed as open, because the Gabbema Gasthuis is a historic almshouse (like Leeuwarden's Sint Anthony Gasthuis, whose own trees are blocked on this site as explicitly private) and no source states in so many words that the grounds are public; treat the access note on the page as 'visible from the street, exact access unconfirmed.'
trees.transport: About 1.2 km east of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flat, tiered branches and the dark evergreen needles, unlike anything else on the street. It stands in front of the Gabbema Gasthuis at Wijbrand de Geeststraat 42, visible from the pavement.

trees.name: The Leaning Black Locust of Westerpark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 100 to 104 years, from a documented planting date of 1924

location.address: Westerpark (Vosseparkje), near Westersingel 8

trees.story:
Leeuwarden's own walking brochure does not lead on this tree's species. It calls it the leaning, propped-up acacia, and it mentions it twice.

The tree is a black locust, white acacia in Dutch, planted in 1924 in Westerpark, the small park at the west edge of the old town that everybody here calls the Vosseparkje. It has spent a century going over sideways and is now carried by a support. That is less alarming than it sounds. Black locusts lean: the timber is famously hard and rot-resistant, the crowns grow heavy and lopsided, and old ones tilt. Nobody has published a verdict on how much longer it has, and it would be wrong to guess in either direction.

The park around it was laid out in 1872 around a drinking-water reservoir the city needed rather more than it needed a park, and the acacia arrived half a century after that. Its neighbours are worth the extra five minutes: a grey poplar planted in 1909 on the east bank of the pond, and across the park a Caucasian wingnut from the Caspian forests with a trunk over a metre round.

Our pin is a park-edge approximation taken from Westersingel 8. The tree itself stands inside the park, and it is the one you cannot mistake.
verified_sources: https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (HCL 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', top-10 entry VIII and its own Westerpark stop 16)
trees.access: Free. Stands in Westerpark (Vosseparkje), an open public park, near its Westersingel 8 edge.
trees.transport: About 1.3 km west of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lean and the support holding it up, which no other tree in this park has. It stands in Westerpark, the Vosseparkje, near the Westersingel edge, on the same side as the 1909 grey poplar.

best_time.label: June, when the acacia hangs full of white flower chains

trees.name: The Silver Lime of Druifstreek
trees.age_estimate: not documented

location.address: Druifstreek, opposite Blokhuispoort

trees.story:
In a breeze this tree changes colour. A silver lime carries dark green leaves that are covered underneath in white felt, so a gust turns the whole crown pale for a second and then back again.

That is exactly why the local IVN nature volunteers put it on their monumental-trees walk through the city. The felt is the field mark that separates Tilia tomentosa from the common lime lining half the streets in this country, including Leeuwarden's own two royal limes, one on the Raadhuisplein and one on the Jacobijnerkerkhof. This is not one of those. It is a southeast European tree, from the Balkans and Anatolia, planted in northern cities because it copes with hard ground and dry summers better than the native limes do.

It stands on the Druifstreek, opposite the Blokhuispoort, on a stretch of the old centre people walk without looking up. The same IVN walk names a second silver lime a few hundred metres north on the Eewal, so once you have learned the leaf you can collect the pair in ten minutes.

Nobody has dated this one. No register carries it, no source gives a planting year, and nobody has taped the trunk. If you know when it went in, or you have a tape measure and thirty seconds, tell us.
trees.access: Free. Stands on Druifstreek, a public city-centre street opposite the Blokhuispoort complex.
trees.transport: About 700 m south of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by turning a leaf over: white felt underneath, dark green on top, where the city's common limes are green on both sides. It stands on the Druifstreek, opposite the Blokhuispoort.
trees.why_go: It is a silver lime rather than another common lime, which is the difference between a street tree and a tree worth stopping at: the leaves are white-felted underneath, so the whole crown flickers pale in a breeze. The local nature volunteers put it on their walk for exactly that.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of Eewal
trees.age_estimate: not documented

location.address: Eewal, opposite Restaurant Spinoza

trees.story:
Silver limes flower in July, when most other nectar in a Dutch city is finished, and it is common to find dead and dying bumblebees on the ground beneath one. For a century the tree's nectar was blamed for poisoning them. The explanation now generally preferred is simpler and sadder: this is the last thing in flower, worn-out bees come to it late, and by then there is not enough in it to save them.

This is one of two silver limes the local IVN nature volunteers put on their monumental-trees walk through Leeuwarden. It stands on the Eewal, opposite Restaurant Spinoza at number 50, in the old centre. The other is a few hundred metres south on the Druifstreek. Both are Tilia tomentosa rather than the common lime of most Dutch streets, and the way to tell is to turn a leaf over: white felt underneath, dark green above.

Nobody has dated this one either. It appears in no national register and no source gives a planting year. If you know when it went in, tell us.

Two independent geocodes for this address agree within about fifteen metres, so the pin will put you on the right frontage rather than at the exact trunk.
trees.access: Free. Stands on Eewal, a public city-centre street opposite Restaurant Spinoza (Eewal 50).
trees.transport: About 800 m south of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaf: white felt underneath, dark green on top, where the city's common limes are green on both sides. It stands on the Eewal, opposite Restaurant Spinoza at number 50.
trees.why_go: A silver lime rather than the common lime of every other Dutch street, with white-felted leaves that turn the crown pale in a breeze, and a July flowering that comes after almost everything else in the city has finished.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of the Harmonie
trees.age_estimate: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820

location.address: Beside the main entrance of Theater De Harmonie, Ruiterskwartier, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682933, London Plane, planted band 1810-1820)
https://periodieken.historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/issue/TKK/1991-06-01/edition/null/page/3 ('t Kleine Krantsje, 1 June 1991, readers' letters page)
trees.access: Free. Stands on the public square beside the theatre's main entrance.
trees.transport: Central Leeuwarden, short walk from Leeuwarden Centraal station.
trees.verify_notes: Register nr 1682933, planted band 1810-1820, next to the main entrance of Theater/Stadsschouwburg De Harmonie. A 1991 letters-page item in 't Kleine Krantsje (a Leeuwarden local-history periodical, HCL's own digitised archive) independently names this exact tree: it calls it 'de meer dan honderd jaar oude plataan bij de Harmonie' (the plane tree by the Harmonie, more than a hundred years old) and describes it as the subject of public concern in 1991 over renovation works that threatened to remove it, with the writer hoping the council would yield to public pressure, drawing a parallel to an old beech at the Princessehof saved by protest decades earlier (that beech, register nr 1682922, was ultimately felled in 2015 per the register, so the parallel held only for a while). The register's 2024 edition carries no removal note for this plane, unlike the Princessehof beeches which explicitly do, so treat it as standing. No girth or exact height found this pass.
trees.story:
In 1991 a reader wrote in to a Leeuwarden local-history paper to defend this tree. Renovation work at De Harmonie was expected to take out the plane beside the main entrance, and the letter asked the council to give way to public pressure, as it had done decades earlier over an old beech at the Princessehof. The plane is still standing. The beech is not. The register records it as felled in 2015, so the precedent held for a while and then it did not.

The letter called it the plane by the Harmonie, more than a hundred years old, which undersold it considerably. The national register of monumental trees puts its planting between 1810 and 1820, closer to two centuries than to one. That band brackets the end of French rule in the Netherlands, which fell away in 1813, so the tree was a sapling in a city that had just changed countries.

Everything around it has changed use at least once since. The tree has not moved, and it still holds the corner of the square where people queue to get into a show. Nobody has recorded a girth or a height for it, which is a gap a tape measure and one message would close.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flaking patchwork bark that only a plane has, cream over olive where the old plates come away. It stands on the public square at the Ruiterskwartier, right beside the main entrance of Theater De Harmonie.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Blokhuispoort
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Keizersgracht / Oosterkade, beside the former Huis van Bewaring (Blokhuispoort)

trees.access: Free. Stands on the public quay/street beside the former Huis van Bewaring at Blokhuispoort, on the Keizersgracht/Oosterkade side of the complex (a different corner from the Crimean linden already on this site, lee_022, which stands at the Blokhuisplein entrance about 550m away).
trees.transport: About 700 m southeast of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.verify_notes: Register nr 1682930. The Blokhuispoort complex began as a 15th-century citadel (Blokhuis), gained a cell wing in 1892-1894 when this chestnut was likely planted, and is now a public library, cultural venue and shops. The register notes sulphur-tuft fungus (zwavelkopjeszwam, a white-rot fungus) found at the base at a 2017-ish inspection but rates the tree's condition as good and says it can safely remain. It also notes the growing site has increasingly been used as a car park, with only a small green strip on the canal side. No second independent source found this pass; single-sourced on the register. Only about 550m from lee_022 (Crimean Linden, Blokhuisplein), a different tree at a different corner of the same historic complex.
trees.story:
This chestnut spent most of its life outside a prison and now stands outside a library.

The Blokhuispoort started as a fifteenth-century citadel, the blokhuis the name comes from, and became the Huis van Bewaring, the city house of detention. Its cell wing went up between 1892 and 1894. The register dates the chestnut to somewhere between 1880 and 1890, so it was in the ground before the masons arrived, and it kept its corner while the cells filled and emptied for the better part of a century. The doors are open now. The complex holds the public library, workspaces and shops, and the walls are one of the few places in Leeuwarden where you can read a book where people once were not allowed to leave.

Inspectors found sulphur tuft at the foot of the trunk, a white-rot fungus, at a check around 2017. They rated the tree good anyway and concluded it can safely stay. The ground has been less generous than the inspectors: the register notes that the growing space has increasingly gone over to parked cars, leaving a thin green strip on the canal side.

About a hundred and forty years of that, and it still drops conkers every autumn. Only the register has written this one up, so if you know more of its story, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the horse chestnut hand of five to seven leaflets spreading from one stalk, and by the cars parked to its foot. It stands on the Keizersgracht quay side of the Blokhuispoort, not at the Blokhuisplein entrance.

best_time.label: late September into October, when the conkers come down on the quay
